title: First Apartment
learning_objectives: Make trade-offs between comfort and affordability

events.description: You're moving into your first apartment with $1,500/month income. Apartment A: $700/month, close to work (saves on transport). Apartment B: $550/month, farther out (bus pass needed, $75/month). Apartment C: $850/month, includes utilities. Where do you live?

choices.label: Apartment A — $700, walk to work
choices.effect: No transport costs! $800 left for everything else. Location saves you time and money.

choices.label: Apartment B — $550 + $75 bus = $625 total
choices.effect: Cheapest housing+transport combo! $875 left. The commute is longer but the savings are real.

choices.label: Apartment C — $850, utilities included
choices.effect: No surprise utility bills! Predictable costs. $650 left for food, savings, and personal.

events.description: Groceries and food. Cooking at home costs about $200/month. Eating out averages $400/month. A mix is around $300/month. How do you plan your food budget?

choices.label: Mostly cook — $200/month + $50 occasional dining
choices.effect: $250 on food. Takes time but saves the most money. Meal prep Sundays help!

choices.label: Cook weekdays, eat out weekends — $300/month
choices.effect: A balanced approach! Home cooking for savings, dining out for socializing.

choices.label: Mostly prepared meals and takeout — $400/month
choices.effect: Saves time but costs more. If your schedule is packed, convenience has value too.

events.description: You need to set a savings target. Financial advisors suggest saving at least 10-20% of income. That's $150-$300/month from your $1,500. But you also want spending money for fun. How much do you save?

choices.label: 20% — $300/month into savings
choices.effect: Aggressive saving! In 6 months you'll have an $1,800 emergency fund. That's financial security.

choices.label: 10% — $150/month, more flexibility
choices.effect: Steady saving with room for fun! $900 emergency fund in 6 months. Balanced approach.

choices.label: 15% — $225/month, middle ground
choices.effect: Right in the sweet spot! $1,350 saved in 6 months. Solid financial foundation.

events.description: Month 2 surprise: your car needs a $400 repair (or bus pass goes up $25/month permanently). How do you handle it?

choices.label: Use your savings — this is what it's for
choices.effect: Emergency fund to the rescue! This is exactly why saving matters. Rebuild it over the next few months.

choices.label: Ask the mechanic for a 3-month payment plan
choices.effect: $133/month for 3 months. Spreads the cost but reduces your flexibility short-term.

choices.label: Cut personal spending this month to cover it
choices.effect: A tight month but you handled it without touching savings! Discipline pays off.

events.description: End of Month 3. Let's review your budget. Are you spending less than you earn? Do you have savings growing? What would you adjust?

choices.label: I'm on track — small tweaks only
choices.effect: Three months of budgeting practice! You've built a sustainable system. Minor adjustments keep it working.

choices.label: I need more income — look for a side gig
choices.effect: Recognizing the income side of the equation! A weekend gig could add $200-400/month.

choices.label: Major restructure — move or change habits
choices.effect: Big changes sometimes make the biggest impact. A cheaper apartment or meal prep could save hundreds.

recap_template: You built a real-world monthly budget from scratch! You balanced rent, food, transport, savings, and surprises. Budgeting isn't about restriction — it's about making your money work for your goals.
positive_framing_rules: Never say the student is struggling financially
Frame budget constraints as decisions, not deprivation
Celebrate awareness and adjustment, not just saving
ai_variation_allowed: Change the city and cost of living

title: Summer Savings + Interest
learning_objectives: Project future value of current decisions

events.description: Summer job! You earn $400/week for 12 weeks ($4,800 total). You found a savings account offering 5% annual interest, compounded monthly. If you save $200/week, after 3 months you'd have about $2,430 (the extra $30 is interest). How much do you save weekly?

choices.label: Save $200/week (50%) — project: ~$2,430 in 3 months
choices.effect: Half saved! At 5% APR compounded monthly, $2,400 grows to about $2,430 in 3 months. Interest starts small but builds!

choices.label: Save $300/week (75%) — project: ~$3,645 in 3 months
choices.effect: Aggressive saving! $3,600 total deposits. With compound interest, you'll have about $3,645. Every dollar earns more dollars!

choices.label: Save $100/week (25%) — project: ~$1,215 in 3 months
choices.effect: Steady saving with plenty of spending money! $1,200 grows to about $1,215. A balanced approach.

events.description: Week 4: Your friend says 'Why bother with 5% interest? It's only like $30 over the summer.' Are they right? Let's think long-term. If you kept that $2,400 in the account for 5 years at 5% compounded monthly, it would grow to about $3,080.

choices.label: That's $680 in free money over 5 years! Keep saving!
choices.effect: Long-term thinking! $680 from interest alone — money making money. And if you keep adding...

choices.label: What if I found a higher interest rate?
choices.effect: Great question! At 7%, that same $2,400 grows to ~$3,400 in 5 years. Rate shopping matters!

choices.label: What about investing in stocks instead?
choices.effect: Stocks historically return ~10% long-term but with more risk. $2,400 could become ~$3,865 in 5 years — but could also drop temporarily.

events.description: Week 8: A concert you've been dreaming about costs $150. You've saved $1,600 so far. If you skip the concert, that $150 saved at 5% for 10 years becomes about $247. What do you do?

choices.label: Skip it — $247 future value is worth it
choices.effect: Delayed gratification! That $150 works for you over the next decade.

choices.label: Go — some experiences are priceless
choices.effect: Memories matter too! Financial planning should leave room for things you love.

choices.label: Find cheaper tickets or split with a friend
choices.effect: Creative! $75 for the experience, $75 stays invested. Best of both worlds.

events.description: End of summer! Let's project forward. If you save $2,400 each summer for 4 years (college summers) at 5% compounded monthly, what would you have at graduation?

choices.label: Let me figure this out — about $10,400!
choices.effect: Close! With compound interest on rolling deposits, you'd have about $10,500. Four summers of discipline = a real financial cushion!

choices.label: I'd set up automatic transfers so I never miss
choices.effect: Automation removes willpower from the equation! 'Pay yourself first' is the #1 savings strategy.

choices.label: I'd try to save more each summer as I earn more
choices.effect: Increasing contributions accelerates compound growth! If you add 10% more each year, you'd have over $11,500!

recap_template: You learned how compound interest turns small savings into real wealth over time! The key insight: time in the market matters more than timing the market. Start early, stay consistent.
positive_framing_rules: Never shame spending on experiences or fun
Frame saving as empowering, not restrictive
Present investing concepts without promoting risk-taking
ai_variation_allowed: Change the job type and income
Vary the interest rates and scenarios

title: Side Hustle Simulator
learning_objectives: Make investment decisions for business growth

events.description: You have $200 to start a side hustle. Option A: Lawn mowing — mower costs $150, charge $25/lawn, gas costs $3/lawn. Option B: Tutoring — $0 startup, charge $20/hour, 5 hours/week available. Option C: Custom stickers — printer ink $50, sticker paper $30, sell for $3 each. Which do you start?

choices.label: Lawn mowing — $22 profit per lawn
choices.effect: Mower bought! $50 left. You need 7 lawns to break even on the mower. After that, it's $22 profit per lawn!

choices.label: Tutoring — $0 startup, immediate profit
choices.effect: Pure profit from day one! $100/week potential. No equipment risk, but limited to your available hours.

choices.label: Custom stickers — $80 startup, scalable
choices.effect: $80 invested, $120 left. Each sticker costs about $0.50 to make and sells for $3. That's a 500% markup!

events.description: Month 1 results are in! You've been working hard. Now you have a choice: reinvest profits to grow, or pocket the earnings. Growing means spending money to make more money.

choices.label: Reinvest 50% of profits
choices.effect: Half back into the business! Better equipment/marketing means more customers next month.

choices.label: Reinvest everything — grow fast
choices.effect: All-in on growth! No pocket money this month but next month's revenue could double.

choices.label: Keep all profits — business stays the same size
choices.effect: Money in your pocket! The business stays at current capacity. Sustainable and steady.

events.description: Month 3: A competitor appears, offering the same service for 20% less. Your customers are asking about it. What's your strategy?

choices.label: Match their prices to keep customers
choices.effect: Price matching keeps customers but cuts your margin. Volume becomes more important.

choices.label: Keep prices but add extra value (better quality, faster service)
choices.effect: Premium positioning! Some customers leave, but loyal ones stay for the quality. Higher margin, fewer customers.

choices.label: Specialize — find a niche they don't serve
choices.effect: Smart differentiation! You found an underserved market. Less competition, loyal customers.

events.description: Month 6 review: you've earned consistently. A friend wants to partner and split the work AND profits 50/50. They'd bring $300 in equipment. Is the partnership worth it?

choices.label: Partner — double capacity, shared profits
choices.effect: With two people, you can take on twice as much work. Revenue could grow faster than the 50% split costs.

choices.label: Hire them at $15/hour instead — keep ownership
choices.effect: You keep control and most of the profit. They earn a wage. Clear boundaries!

choices.label: Stay solo — you've got a good thing going
choices.effect: Independence! Your business, your rules, your profits. Growth will be slower but it's all yours.

events.description: Year-end projection! Based on your choices, let's calculate your total profit and hourly rate. Was the hustle worth it compared to a regular part-time job at $15/hour?

choices.label: My effective hourly rate is higher — worth it!
choices.effect: Entrepreneurship paid more per hour! Plus you gained business skills no job could teach.

choices.label: About the same money, but I learned a lot more
choices.effect: The skills — pricing, marketing, customer service, cash flow — are worth more than the extra dollars.

choices.label: I'd try a different hustle next time with what I learned
choices.effect: Iteration! Every entrepreneur's second business is better than their first. You've got the playbook now.

recap_template: You ran a side hustle for 6 months! You learned about startup costs, profit margins, competition, and growth decisions. Entrepreneurship is about solving problems and creating value.
positive_framing_rules: Never say the business is failing
Frame competition as a healthy part of business
Celebrate learning from all outcomes, not just profit

title: College Cost Planner
learning_objectives: Compare total cost of education options
Calculate projected ROI of different paths

events.description: College planning! Option A: State university — $12,000/year (after aid). Option B: Community college 2 years ($4,000/year) then transfer to state ($12,000/year x 2). Option C: Private university — $30,000/year (but $15,000 scholarship, so $15,000/year). Total costs: A=$48,000, B=$32,000, C=$60,000. You have $5,000 saved. What's your plan?

choices.label: State university — $48,000 over 4 years
choices.effect: Full campus experience! $48,000 total. After $5,000 savings, you need $43,000 in loans/work/aid.

choices.label: Community college + transfer — $32,000 total
choices.effect: Smartest financial move! Same degree, $16,000 less than Option A. After savings, $27,000 needed.

choices.label: Private university — $60,000 (with scholarship)
choices.effect: Premium education, premium cost. The scholarship helps but $55,000 is still a lot. What's the career earning potential?

events.description: Loan time. Federal student loans charge about 5% interest. If you borrow $40,000, the standard 10-year repayment means ~$424/month ($50,880 total — you pay $10,880 in interest). How do you minimize borrowing?

choices.label: Work part-time during school — earn $5,000/year
choices.effect: $20,000 less in loans! Total borrowing drops to $20,000. Monthly payment becomes ~$212. Much more manageable!

choices.label: Apply for 10 scholarships — average $2,000 each if you win 3
choices.effect: Scholarship effort pays off! $6,000 in scholarships reduces loans by 15%. Every application is worth the time.

choices.label: Work summers and save aggressively
choices.effect: 3 summers x $4,000 saved = $12,000 less borrowing. Combined with your initial $5,000, that's significant!

events.description: Let's talk ROI. The average state university graduate earns $55,000/year starting salary. Community college transfer grads earn the same (same degree!). Private university grads average $62,000 starting. Over 10 years, which path has the best return?

choices.label: CC transfer — lowest cost, same salary as state = best ROI
choices.effect: Correct! Same $55k salary but $16k less in costs. The ROI math strongly favors this path.

choices.label: Private — $7,000/year more salary might offset the higher cost
choices.effect: Over 10 years, $70,000 extra earnings vs $28,000 extra cost. Net benefit of $42,000! But only if you get that salary.

choices.label: It depends on my field — some careers need specific schools
choices.effect: Nuanced thinking! In some fields, school prestige matters more. In others, the degree itself is what counts. Research your specific career path.

events.description: Final question: you got into your top choice AND received unexpected financial aid reducing costs by $8,000/year. But your second choice offers a full-ride scholarship (free tuition). What do you choose?

choices.label: Top choice with partial aid — follow your dream
choices.effect: Your dream school, more affordable now! The reduced cost makes the loan burden manageable.

choices.label: Full ride — graduate debt-free
choices.effect: Zero debt at graduation! That financial freedom means more choices after college. Grad school, travel, or save immediately.

choices.label: Use the full-ride offer to negotiate with top choice
choices.effect: Smart! Many schools will match or improve offers. Your top choice increases aid by $3,000/year.

recap_template: You planned for college costs using loans, scholarships, work, and ROI analysis! Education is an investment — understanding the math helps you make the best choice for your future.
positive_framing_rules: Never say a school choice is wrong or too expensive
Frame loans as tools, not traps
ai_variation_allowed: Change the school types and costs
